function_analysis: Stored functions F1-F5 apply. This round asks again for sub-micron flow redirection (now with animal origin), for a plant-derived sub-micron lattice that insulates and shades, and for a self-renewing white coat whose renewal is driven by something more reliable than rain in hot climates.

requirements.name: indoor_heat_gain_reduction
requirements.criterion: Clearly lowers the summer-day heat flux into the interior (roughly >20 %) versus the aged conventional white cool coating on the same envelope.

requirements.name: fully_passive
requirements.criterion: Works without electricity, pumps, fans or water supply; only sun, sky, wind and rain act on it.

requirements.name: weather_durability_20yr
requirements.criterion: Keeps its optical and thermal function (and adhesion) for at least 20 years under hot-climate UV, thermal cycling, rain, dust/sand and soiling without major maintenance.

requirements.name: bionic_mechanism
requirements.criterion: The working mechanism is actually derived from a biological model (plant, animal, microbe), not only labelled so.

requirements.name: building_practicality
requirements.criterion: Applicable as coating or facade structure on real buildings at acceptable cost, weight and glare, without toxic release.

analogues_considered: Balsa/wood cell walls: aligned cellulose nanofibril lattice; delignified 'nanowood' is white, strong and transversely insulating (k ~0.03 W/mK)
Desert plant leaf pubescence (Encelia farinosa): white hairs reflect sunlight and hold still air
Birch bark: sacrificial renewal of a white outer layer
Photo-chalking of anatase-pigmented paints: UV-paced surface renewal
Animal microstructures in the viscous sublayer (shark denticles, bird feather barbules) act only at 10 um-mm scale
objective_statement: Summer-day (24 h) heat flux into the conditioned interior through the sun-exposed roof and facades of a building in a hot climate, averaged over a 20-year service life, including UV ageing, weathering and soiling of the outer surface (not the value of a freshly applied clean surface).
baseline_statement: Conventional white acrylic/elastomeric cool-roof or facade coating (initial solar reflectance ~0.85, thermal emittance ~0.90) in its in-service aged and soiled condition (3-year aged solar reflectance ~0.65-0.70, as in CRRC ageing data), repainted every ~10 years, on the same insulated wall or roof.

candidates.infeasibility_reason: As for the plant variant of this cell: sub-micron features lie deep inside the viscous sublayer of the wind boundary layer (roughness Reynolds number ~1e-2), where Stokes flow cannot be redirected, so no sub-micron flow-redirection structure of any origin can change convective heat transfer; flow-steering features must be mm to m in size.

candidates.title: Nanowood white insulating facade panel
candidates.summary: A 20 mm facade panel of delignified, hydrophobised wood ('nanowood') whose aligned cellulose nanofibril lattice, inherited from the wood cell wall, scatters sunlight (white, SR ~0.85-0.9), emits in the mid-IR and conducts heat very poorly across the fibres (~0.03 W/mK). One plant-made lattice therefore shades like the spine pile and insulates like the aerogel mat.

back_of_envelope.quantity: Reduction of daily-mean west-facade heat flux vs aged white paint on the wall

candidates.main_risk: Unprotected cellulose outdoors swells, grows mould and photo-yellows; even hydrophobised nanowood is unlikely to keep its whiteness and strength for 20 years in sun and rain.
candidates.novelty_vs_known: Closest known: radiative-cooling wood and nanowood insulation from the laboratory (2018-2019), and conventional ETICS; new is using one plant lattice as a combined white skin and insulating facade panel.
candidates.baseline: Conventional white acrylic facade coating, aged and soiled (SR 0.67, emittance 0.90), directly on the same insulated wall.
candidates.inspiration_source: Wood (balsa, basswood) cell walls: aligned cellulose nanofibrils (~20-50 nm) in a lattice of hollow cells; after lignin removal the lattice is white by scattering and transversely insulating.
candidates.physical_mechanism: Aligned cellulose nanofibrils with ~50 % air in sub-micron gaps scatter sunlight and phonon-scatter heat across the fibre direction, giving k_perp ~0.03 W/mK; cellulose emits strongly at 8-13 um. Steady 1D series conduction through wall and panel with sol-air Robin boundary.

parameters.name: panel_conductivity
parameters.justification: Nanowood transverse k 0.03 W/mK dry; wetting raises it.

parameters.name: panel_solar_reflectance_aged
parameters.justification: Clean ~0.9; photo-yellowing and soiling lower it.

candidates.title: UV-paced photo-chalking birch-bark coat
candidates.summary: A thick white silicate coat with 5 vol% of an organic co-binder and anatase TiO2 at the grain surfaces: sunlight's UV photo-oxidises the co-binder in the top micrometres at a rate set by the UV dose, releasing a thin, white chalk layer that takes the deposited dirt with it and exposes fresh surface, like birch bark shedding its outer layer. Unlike rain erosion, the UV dose varies by only ~30 % between hot climates, and the anatase also oxidises organic soot on the surface.

back_of_envelope.quantity: Reduction of service-life-mean roof heat flux vs aged white acrylic cool coating
back_of_envelope.formula: Chalking rate ~5-10 um/yr (anatase chalking paints in Florida/Arizona), steady dirt load ~1/3 of acrylic's -> life-mean SR ~0.82 (clean 0.90), eps 0.92, vs baseline life-mean 0.70: q = 0.5*(54 + 150 - 78.2)/15.5 = 4.06 vs 5.27 W/m2 -> -23 %

candidates.main_risk: Chalk and dirt need wind or rain to leave the surface; the loose chalk rubs off and stains, and photocatalysis attacks sealants and adjacent organic materials.
candidates.novelty_vs_known: Closest known: historic chalking anatase paints and photocatalytic silicate facade paints; new is a thick, fully white reserve coat whose renewal rate is designed from the UV dose for 20 years, instead of relying on rain erosion.
candidates.baseline: Conventional white acrylic cool coating, aged and soiled (life-mean SR ~0.70 with repaint every 10 years, emittance 0.90), on the same roof.
candidates.inspiration_source: Birch (Betula) bark: the white outer phellem is continuously sacrificed and replaced from below, so the surface stays white regardless of what lands on it.
candidates.physical_mechanism: UV (300-400 nm) is absorbed within ~1-2 um by anatase; photogenerated radicals oxidise the organic co-binder, so the grains in the top layer lose cohesion at a rate v = (absorbed UV photon flux x quantum yield x molar volume of co-binder)/co-binder fraction, typically 5-10 um/yr; the white chalk is removed by wind and rain with the deposited dirt. Modelled as steady advection-diffusion of absorbing dirt in the receding surface layer with the UV-derived erosion velocity; the steady dirt load sets absorptance in the sol-air roof balance.

parameters.name: uv_photon_flux_annual_mean
parameters.justification: 300-400 nm photon flux ~ 1e20 /m2/s at noon, ~1.7e19 annual mean in hot climates.

parameters.name: quantum_yield_cobinder_oxidation
parameters.justification: Effective yield for binder scission in anatase paints (most carriers recombine).

parameters.name: cobinder_volume_fraction
parameters.justification: Just enough organic co-binder to give cohesion before chalking.

parameters.name: cobinder_molar_volume
parameters.justification: Per oxidised repeat unit of an acrylic co-binder.

parameters.name: clean_solar_reflectance
parameters.justification: Anatase/rutile-free BaSO4/CaCO3 white; anatase absorbs UV (~4 % of solar).
